title: TLAC's Advocacy Partnerships Lessons from Our 2026 Panel Discussion scussion/
author: Brittany Hargrove
summary: Brittany Hargrove, Teach Like a Champion's Director of Advocacy and Partnerships, recaps a June 2026 panel that gathered TLAC's advocacy partners to discuss how to help new and novice teachers and leaders thrive and stay in the profession. The post frames TLAC's mission as codifying replicable teaching techniques so more classrooms become places where children reach their potential, and positions partner organizations as a window into the needs of educators entering the field, especially in under-served communities. Three insights organize the piece. First, apprenticeship accelerates development when novices are paired with experts, receive regular observation and feedback, and have clear growth goals, closing what one panelist called the gap between aspiration and apprenticeship. Second, relational and adaptive skills, including reframing classroom management as building a productive classroom environment, are becoming as essential as content knowledge. Third, sustaining conditions such as clear priorities, embedded collaboration, strong adult systems, shared instructional language, internal video of colleagues' practice, and sincere appreciation can be deliberately built to move teachers from survival to sustainability. It closes with TLAC's commitments to expand apprenticeships and study relational moments on classroom video.
points: Partners argue novice teachers flourish through apprenticeship: models, timely feedback, and real practice in the moves and routines of the classroom rather than one-off workshops.
Chatham University anchors senior education majors' capstone research in relationship building so new secondary teachers learn that the work begins with loving the students, not just the content.
Reframing 'classroom management' as creating a productive classroom environment emphasizes predictable, trusting spaces where students buy in because the teacher believes in them.
Raymie Fernandez names five sustaining conditions: clarity of priorities, embedded collaboration, strong adult systems, belonging paired with accountability, and proximity to one's own impact.
Shanti Bhavan uses internal classroom video and a shared instructional language to combat burnout by letting teachers see techniques working in their own community.
quotes: The purpose was simple: to pull our partners close and learn from their experiences, so we can better anticipate and respond to the challenges they, and other organizations doing this necessary work, face in their support of new and novice teachers. The conversation was centered on a question we’re always grappling with, “How can we best support new and novice teachers and leaders so they can thrive in the profession, positively impacting their school communities for as long as possible?

Apprenticeships Accelerate Development: Apprenticeships accelerate development when novice teachers are paired with expert practitioners, provided regular observation/feedback cycles, and have clearly defined goals for their growth. Relational and Adaptive Skills are Critical: Relational and adaptive skills are critical to building classrooms where students feel seen, safe, and valued. Nurturing and Supportive Conditions Must Be Intentionally Shaped: Nurturing and supportive conditions protect and sustain teachers when built with intention. Apprenticeships Accelerate Development

Their answers were energizing, the educators they work with are deeply committed, and the opportunity is to match that commitment with deliberate apprenticeship into the actual moves, routines, and decisions that make classrooms and school campuses thrive. Raymie Fernandez from the National Fellowship for Black and Latino Male Educators framed the goal beautifully as closing the gap between aspiration and apprenticeship. Teachers and leaders flourish when they get models, timely feedback, and real chances to practice the work.

Many new secondary teachers arrive loving their content, and Chatham helps them discover that the work begins with loving the kids, anchoring senior education majors’ capstone research in relationship building so they practice connecting with students and reflect on what works. Relational and Adaptive Skills are Critical

Neal Currie, founder of Teach Brother Teach, described teaching as a fundamentally human endeavor, where the highest leverage skills are relationship building, cultural responsiveness, reflection, and helping students think critically. Students learn best, he reminded us, when they feel seen, valued, and connected. Our Jamaica Peace Corps partners described a similar blend for today’s classrooms: digital literacy, social emotional skills, student centered methods, and the habit of belonging to a community of practice where teachers learn from one another.

Cunningham (Chatham University) offered a reframe we loved, shifting from the term classroom management to creating a productive classroom environment. It is a move toward building the kind of predictable, trusting space where students buy in because they know their teacher believes in their success. Nurturing and Supportive Conditions Must Be Intentionally Shaped

His aspiration, beautifully put, is to help educators move from survival to disciplined sustainability, doing the work they love, over time. Gabrielle Mahesh and Codi Canton from Shanti Bhavan shared that they are working toward a shared instructional language so that teachers can focus their energy with clear, consistent expectations.

Gabby and Codi also named the power of showcasing internal video in showing teachers their growth to combat burnout. Teachers having an opportunity to see their own students and colleagues apply techniques in their own community has been immensely powerful and inspiring. S.
